questions.text: What is the research question?
questions.help: The aim of the analysis usually matters more than the shape of the data. A causal analysis and a prediction model use different covariates and different quality measures.

options.label: Describe
options.help: How common a disease is, how a measurement is distributed.

options.label: Estimate the effect of an exposure or a treatment
options.help: Does drug A reduce mortality compared with drug B? Does smoking increase the risk of stroke?

options.label: Predict an outcome for the individual patient
options.help: Develop or validate a risk, diagnostic or prognostic model.

options.label: Assess the accuracy of a diagnostic test
options.help: Sensitivity and specificity of a test against a reference standard.

options.label: Combine the results of several studies (meta-analysis)
options.help: Pool the effect estimates of published or shared studies.

options.label: Measure agreement or reliability
options.help: Do two instruments or two raters give the same result?

questions.text: Does the model predict a current state or a future event?

options.label: Current state (diagnosis)
options.help: Does the patient have the disease now?

options.label: Future event (prognosis)
options.help: Will the patient have the event within a given time?

questions.text: What is the study design?

options.label: Randomised cross-over trial
options.help: Each participant receives the treatments in sequence, with a wash-out period between them.

options.label: Routinely collected data (electronic health records, registries, administrative databases)

questions.text: What does the trial aim to show?

options.label: That a treatment is not worse by more than a margin (non-inferiority)
That two treatments are equivalent within a margin (equivalence)

questions.text: What type of outcome variable do you have?

options.label: Continuous
options.help: Blood pressure, cholesterol, length of stay.

options.label: Binary
options.help: Yes or no: died, recovered, admitted to hospital.

options.label: Ordinal
options.help: Ordered categories: stage I-IV, modified Rankin scale.

options.label: Nominal with more than 2 categories
options.help: Categories with no order: tumour type.

options.label: Count or rate
options.help: Number of exacerbations, number of emergency visits.

options.label: Time to event
options.help: Time to death, relapse or admission, with censored patients.

questions.text: How common is the outcome in the study population?
What type of measurement do you want to compare?

options.label: Continuous
options.help: Two devices that measure blood pressure.

options.label: Categorical or ordinal
options.help: Two radiologists who classify the same images.

questions.text: Are the observations independent?
questions.help: Repeated measurements on the same patient, or patients from the same hospital, are correlated.

options.label: Paired or matched (before and after, matched pairs, matched case-control)
Repeated measurements over time on the same subject

questions.text: Are there events that prevent the event of interest?
questions.help: For example, if the outcome is cardiovascular death, death from cancer is a competing event.

questions.text: What type is the main exposure?

options.label: Changes over time (a drug started or stopped during follow-up)

questions.text: Are there confounders that change over time and are themselves affected by earlier exposure?
questions.help: Example: blood pressure influences whether a drug is started, and the drug then changes blood pressure.

questions.text: Does the study compare a newer drug with an older one?
questions.help: In routine data, many users of a newer drug have often used the older (comparator) drug before.

options.label: No, the study does not compare two drugs
Yes, and most patients start either drug for the first time
Yes, and many users of the newer drug switched from, or added it to, the older drug

questions.text: Do you plan to use machine learning (random forest, neural networks, SVM)?
Do you plan a Bayesian analysis?
questions.help: A Bayesian analysis combines prior information with the data and reports probabilities of effects.

questions.text: How many subjects are in the dataset?
How many studies do you want to combine?
How many events?
questions.help: For a binary outcome: the number of subjects in the less frequent category. For time to event: the number of observed events.

questions.text: How many parameters do you want to estimate?
questions.help: Count parameters, not columns: a categorical variable with k levels counts k-1, a spline with 3 knots counts 2.

questions.text: How much data is missing?

options.label: A fair amount in the covariates
A fair amount in the outcome

questions.text: Who are the results for?
questions.help: This does not change which model suits the data: it changes what may be useful to show and which formal requirements may apply.
